a-knight-of-the-nineteenth-century: Edward Payson Roe, a minister turned bestselling novelist, wrote fiction meant to uplift as well as entertain. This novel follows a young man determined to live by old ideals of honor in a modern, money-driven age. Through romance, temptation, and hard choices, Roe shows what nineteenth-century knightliness might look like — faith, duty, and courage in everyday life.
simple-italian-cookery: Antonia Isola's cookbook brought real Italian home cooking to English-speaking kitchens in the early 1900s. Its recipes cover pasta, soups, meats, and sweets in straightforward instructions that assume no great skill. More than a recipe list, the book is a delicious record of how Italian families actually ate a century ago.
the-monastery: Walter Scott sets this historical novel in the Scottish Borders during the Reformation, when old Catholic monasteries faced a new Protestant order. The monks of Melrose watch their world crumble while young heroes navigate love and loyalty amid religious upheaval. Rich in Scots character and historical color, it is Scott doing what he did best — bringing a vanished age to life.
once-aboard-the-lugger-the-history-of-ge: A. S. M. Hutchinson, author of the bestseller If Winter Comes, tells a salt-sprayed romance aboard a sailing lugger. George and his Mary find love with the sea around them and adventure close at hand. Leisurely, tender, and full of nautical atmosphere, the novel recalls the age when a good love story was the surest entertainment.
nature-s-serial-story: Edward Payson Roe weaves his love of the natural world into a novel where the changing seasons frame a human love story. Month by month, flowers, birds, and weather mirror the courtship unfolding among his characters. Part romance, part nature diary, the book charmed Victorian readers who liked their fiction sweet and their wildflowers accurately named.
the-law-of-the-land-of-miss-lady-whom-it: Emerson Hough, chronicler of the American West, sets this novel on the frontier where law was still being made. Miss Lady and John Eddring are drawn into mystery and danger in a land settling its accounts. Hough's deep knowledge of western history gives the romance and adventure an authentic ring.
a-handbook-of-ethical-theory: Philosopher George Stuart Fullerton offers students a clear tour of moral philosophy — what makes an act right or wrong, and why thinkers have disagreed for centuries. Duty, happiness, conscience, and character each get careful, fair-minded treatment. Written as a college text, it remains a steady guide for anyone beginning to think seriously about ethics.
mr-world-and-miss-church-member-a-twenti: W. S. Harris writes a modern Pilgrim's Progress for the twentieth century, in which Mr. World courts Miss Church-Member and tempts her from her faith. The allegory warns believers against compromise with worldly pleasures and fashions. Earnest and direct, it spoke to churchgoers worried about the changing morals of the modern age.
haste-and-waste-or-the-young-pilot-of-la: Oliver Optic — the pen name of William Taylor Adams — was the most popular boys' author of his day, and this Lake Champlain tale shows why. A young pilot learns that haste makes waste as he navigates storms, smugglers, and moral choices on the lake. Fast, wholesome, and instructive, it is classic Optic from first page to last.
unconscious-memory: Samuel Butler — the iconoclastic author of Erewhon — argues in this provocative book that heredity is a form of memory passed unconsciously from parent to child. umbrellas-and-their-history: William Sangster tells the odd, gay story of the umbrella — from old Eastern sunshades to the staid Victorian standby. Makers, modes, and merry tales crowd a book that proves no theme too slight for good telling. Daily things, it seems, have the best pasts.
little-memoirs-of-the-nineteenth-century: George Paston — the pen name of Emily Morse Symonds — gathers brief, lively memoirs of notable nineteenth-century figures. Artists, writers, and eccentrics pass in quick, well-drawn sketches. A delightful sampler of Victorian lives, written with the light touch of a born biographer.

Any reader who wants to know why dramas move us should start here.
the-mill-mystery: Anna Katharine Green — called the mother of the American detective novel — spins a classic whodunit around a body found at a lonely mill. govdocs-archive_org-JonBenetRamseyCaseSu:
Chapter twenty of David McGowan's Programmed to Kill, titled Boulder, treats the murder of JonBenet Ramsey, the six-year-old found dead in her Boulder, Colorado home in 1996. McGowan's book argues that many notorious crimes hide organized abuse networks. The Ramsey chapter applies that thesis to America's most debated unsolved case.

McGowan reviews the ransom note, the family's conduct, the police work, and the media storm, reading each through his characteristic conspiratorial lens. His account is argument, not established fact; the case remains officially unsolved and widely disputed. The chapter is held as true-crime writing from the archive, for researchers who study the case and its literature.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HaapinenLarry_H:
Larry Haapinen wrote an article titled Oswald and the U-2, pegged to Francis Gary Powers' book Operation Overflight. Powers was the U-2 pilot shot down over the Soviet Union in 1960. Haapinen's piece discusses Lee Harvey Oswald in connection with the U-2 affair.

Oswald had served as a Marine radar operator and later defected to the Soviet Union, which long fed questions about what he knew. Tying his name to the spy plane story placed the assassin inside Cold War intelligence history. The article preserves that line of speculation as it was argued in print.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HurtHenry_Hurt_:
Chapter Eleven of Henry Hurt's book on the Kennedy assassination takes up the Cuban question. Its title asks the book's central choice: coincidence or conspiracy. In the chapter Hurt quotes the Schweiker Report, a Senate product, and President Lyndon B. Johnson himself.

Cuba sat at the crossroads of the case: Castro's enemies, Oswald's pro-Castro acts, and exile raiders all met there. Hurt weighs whether those crossings were chance or design. A senator's report and a president's words give the chapter its spine, and the excerpt preserves his argument at its most pointed.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PetersenHenry_P:
FBI official A. Evans sent this memorandum to Mr. Belmont on December 17, 1963. Its subject is Henry Petersen of the Justice Department. Petersen worked in the department's Organized Crime and Racketeering Section. He had been asked to serve on the Presidential Commission investigating the Kennedy assassination, the body soon known as the Warren Commission.

Staffing the commission was sensitive work. A Justice Department organized-crime man brought one kind of expertise and one kind of suspicion. The memo records the bureau noting the appointment for its own files. It is a small dated trace of the commission being assembled, less than a month after the assassination, while the FBI watched who would judge its work.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-StoneGregory_St: Los Angeles police oversight took place in public, and the meeting of March 4, 1986, was written down word for word. The transcript covers item 3-A on the agenda of the LAPD Board of Police Commissioners. Verbatim records like this one show how civilian commissioners questioned and directed one of the largest police departments in the country during the 1980s.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Treasury_Treasu: Picture Scoop magazine previewed its contents on a single page, and one item stands out: Henry Morgenthau Jr. writing on Your Money. Morgenthau had been Franklin Roosevelt's Secretary of the Treasury. A contents page is only a promise of articles, but it shows how a photo magazine sold financial advice from a famous name. The November page survives as a small piece of magazine history.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-UnderhillGary_U: J. Garrett Underhill, a former intelligence agent, told friends he knew who killed President Kennedy. Shortly afterward he was shot dead. The article reporting his death treats it as part of the assassination mystery rather than a closed case. Underhill's story became one of the most repeated in assassination research. The piece preserves the claim and the grim end that made it famous.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WPAFilmLibrary_: A Christmas card from MPI Media Group reached Harold Weisberg from his friends at the company. MPI worked with film libraries, including the WPA Film Library named in the file. The card is a small, warm item in a research archive mostly filled with conflict and suspicion. It shows the friendly business ties behind Weisberg's later work in film and publishing.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WegrockiHenry_W: A Baltimore Sun article by Isaac Rehert profiles a young researcher named Henry Wegrocki. Its headline states his belief plainly: the CIA was behind Kennedy's death. Few newspapers gave young critics of the Warren Commission that kind of space in those years. The article shows a mainstream paper presenting a heretical claim through the person who held it, rather than endorsing or crushing it.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_colombia:
A Colombian taxi driver carried secret cash from Chiquita Brands to a right-wing paramilitary group, and in 2023 he received a thirty-six-month prison sentence. This briefing book, posted that April, draws on internal documents from the Archive's Chiquita Papers. They show his role was larger than earlier reports said.

During the 1990s the driver served as a key go-between for the fruit company. He dealt with practically every major armed actor in Colombia's conflict, not just one group. His case turns an abstract corporate crime into a human chain of payments, one bag of cash at a time.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va: The United States and Cyberspace: Military Organization, Policy - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_indonesi:
East Timor voted on independence from Indonesia in a historic 1999 referendum. Brad Simpson edited this briefing book, number 682, marking twenty years since that vote. Declassified documents show what the United States knew in the run-up, and what it chose to protect.

Washington knew the Indonesian military had created, directed, and armed the militias terrorizing East Timor. Their plan was to kill, drive out, or silence independence activists before the vote. Even so, the United States sought to preserve close ties with that military. The gap between knowledge and policy is documented here in the government's own paper.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Anatoly Chernyaev worked inside the Soviet Central Committee and kept a diary that recorded the system talking to itself. Anna Melyakova translated and Svetlana Savranskaya edited this volume, number 830, published in May 2023. The diary covers the year 1983.

Chernyaev complained of his humiliating role, dressing a naked, completely naked king. On the KAL airliner shootdown that year, he wrote that it showcased the power of the military complex over Soviet life and politics. On nuclear war he reflected that a world of human achievement could vanish in a few short minutes. Few sources put a senior insider's private honesty on paper this plainly.

Anatoly Sergeyevich Chernyaev wrote one of the great insider diaries of the late Soviet Union. The Archive published his diary for 1978 in English for the first time in May 2018, on what would have been his ninety-seventh birthday. Svetlana Savranskaya edited the edition.

Chernyaev wrote from inside the Central Committee of the Communist Party, where he then worked. A daily diary at that level records meetings, moods, and doubts that official minutes hide. The 1978 volume predates his years as Gorbachev's aide, which makes it a baseline: the same sharp observer, watching a system that did not yet know it was entering its final decade.

President Bill Clinton traveled to Moscow in January 1994 for a summit with Russian president Boris Yeltsin, barely two years after the Soviet Union collapsed. The National Security Archive briefing book on that meeting publishes declassified transcripts of what the two leaders said to each other behind closed doors.

The talks show close work together on nuclear safety and on regional security problems left over from the Cold War. At the same time, worry grows in the record about Russia's troubled shift to a market system, which was bringing hardship and political strain. Readers see a hopeful partnership in plain language, along with the early signs of the troubles that would later strain it.

Anatoly Chernyaev's diary for 1980 records life inside the Soviet Central Committee while Leonid Brezhnev still ruled. Briefing Book number 706, published in May 2020, presents the diary in Anna Melyakova's translation, edited by Svetlana Savranskaya. The Archive calls its author irreplaceable as a witness to that closed world.

One entry asks who is supposed to answer for Afghanistan, where Soviet troops had invaded the year before. Another notes that most work was done to please one man, Brezhnev, and to disturb him as little as possible. Lines like those show a system run for the comfort of an aging leader. The diary gives readers a rare insider's daily record from behind the Kremlin's walls.

Anatoly Chernyaev wrote his 1984 diary while still waiting for a leader who would change the Soviet Union; Mikhail Gorbachev would take power the next year. Briefing Book number 860 presents that diary, translated and edited by Svetlana Savranskaya with help from Anna Melyakova, as part of the Archive's long project of publishing Chernyaev's private record.

Entries quoted from the diary ask what would happen if the weapons were simply destroyed, full stop. Others call the Afghan war an effort to make a country happy that cost thousands of lives and brought global shame. Chernyaev mocks his own idealism, then sizes up Gorbachev as lively, quick, and able to grasp the essence of things. Few sources show the mood inside the Soviet elite so plainly on the eve of reform.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_colombia-chiquita: Chiquita, the banana company, was found liable in an American court for killings carried out by a Colombian paramilitary group it had paid for years. A National Security Archive briefing book page carries that verdict under a plain headline naming the company and the crime. The case grew from payments Chiquita admitted making to the United Self-Defense Forces of Colombia, a group on the United States terrorist list. Only the page capture survives in this entry's evidence, marking the Archive's record of a landmark corporate accountability judgment.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia-human-rights:
In a forced disappearance case from Bolivia, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ordered the state to open its military archives and guarantee the right to truth. A National Security Archive news post from January 2023 reports the ruling and what it requires of the Bolivian government.

Forced disappearance works by erasing records: the victim vanishes and the state denies everything. An order to open military files attacks that erasure directly, because the archives are where orders, rosters, and reports survive. The court's demand also sets a standard other countries in the region can be measured against. Readers interested in how international courts turn human rights language into concrete duties will find a clear, compact example here.
podcast-dannyjones-nCbtQCikARY:
Bek Lover joins Danny Jones for a talk on God, aliens, and what he calls the demonic realm. Lover is a repeat guest who reads UFO lore through a strong Christian lens. His view ties craft in the sky to spirits in scripture.

Lover argues that so-called aliens are in truth fallen beings from the Bible. He links sightings, abduction tales, and end-times signs into one frame. Jones lets him preach the frame at length, then tests it. Listeners get a faith-first take on the UFO wave. The library files the talk as an archive record of the guest's beliefs.
podcast-joerogan-71XphFGuORY:
Religion professor Diana Walsh Pasulka joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2091. Pasulka wrote American Cosmic, a study of UFO belief drawn from fieldwork with scientists and experiencers. She approaches saucers the way scholars approach faith, which sets her apart from most guests on the topic.

She explains why smart people treat UFO events as sacred, and how tech leaders quietly fund the research. Rogan asks where her study left her own beliefs. The episode offers a rare angle on the phenomenon: not whether the craft are real, but why the stories around them carry such religious weight.
podcast-joerogan-sKwq7mpBTrY:
Congressman Tim Burchett of Tennessee talks UFOs with Joe Rogan in episode 2495 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Burchett is one of the loudest voices in Congress demanding that the government release what it knows. He brings a plain, funny, country style to a topic full of suits.

Burchett describes the pushback he says lawmakers get when they ask about secret programs. He talks about hearings, whistleblowers, and the money trail behind hidden projects. Rogan asks what Burchett himself believes is flying in our skies. The episode gives disclosure a rare insider who speaks like a neighbor, not a press release.
podcast-tuckercarlson-8zPJGAQYMRY:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton joins Tucker Carlson to talk border strain. Carlson calls immigration the state's most pressing problem. It has changed Texas in every way, he says.

Paxton expects new federal orders to bite fast, based on past terms. He recalls politics from the Bush years onward. The title charges that George Soros shields cartels from the law. It also notes Paxton's blacklist by Fox News. Paxton presents himself as a fighter punished for his stands. The episode gives Texas voters his case in full. The fight, he insists, is far from over.
a-strange-story:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton, a star of the Victorian book world, wrote this occult romance in 1862. Its hero is a young doctor drawn to a wise, dark man of great wealth and strange powers. Bulwer-Lytton had a deep taste for the lore of the hidden world.

The tale turns on mesmerism, alchemy, and the search for a drink that grants long life. Love, pride, and dread grow as the young man trades his soul's rest for dark lore. The book was the great public hit of its kind in its age, and it still grips.
mcclellan-own-story:
George McClellan, the Union general who built the Army of the Potomac, died before finishing his memoir. McClellan's Own Story appeared in 1887, set in order by his literary executor. It is his defense of his Civil War command.

McClellan tells of the Peninsula campaign, Antietam, and his removal by Lincoln. He insists that Washington starved him of men and misread the enemy. Critics have long disputed his claims, which is part of the book's interest. Few Civil War memoirs show so clearly how a general argues his case to history. His widow saw the unfinished work through the press after his death.
washington-up-from-slavery:
Booker Washington published Up from Slavery in 1901, and it became the most influential Black memoir of its era. Born enslaved in Virginia, Washington taught himself to read after emancipation. At twenty-five he founded the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama.

He tells of working in salt furnaces and coal mines to reach Hampton Institute. At Tuskegee he built a school from almost nothing, brick by brick, with student labor. His Atlanta speech of 1895, urging work and patience, made him a national figure. Critics then and since have debated his bargain with segregation, but the book's reach is beyond doubt.
geronimo-story:
Geronimo, the Apache war leader, dictated his life story in 1906 while held as a prisoner of war at Fort Sill. S. M. Barrett, a local school official, took down his words with his permission. Geronimo said he wanted the truth told at last.

He recalls his youth in the Southwest, Mexican raids that killed his family, and his long wars against Mexico and the United States. His surrenders, escapes, and final capture in 1886 close the tale. The book gives the Apache wars from the Apache side, in a voice both proud and bitter. Geronimo died still a prisoner three years later.
tudela-itinerary:
Benjamin of Tudela, a Jewish traveler from Navarre, journeyed across the known world in the years around 1160. His Itinerary, in Marcus Adler's translation, reports what he found from Spain to Baghdad and beyond. It is the medieval world's most important travel narrative of its kind.

Benjamin counts Jewish communities in city after city, noting their scholars, trades, and numbers. He also describes Rome, Constantinople, Jerusalem, and Baghdad with a merchant's eye for wealth and power. Tales of distant lands, some fabulous, close the route home. Historians mine the book for facts found nowhere else. Adler's notes trace his route and test his claims against other sources.
mary-prince-history:
Mary Prince dictated The History of Mary Prince in London in 1831. She was the first enslaved Black woman to publish a life narrative in Britain. Anti-slavery allies printed her words while her case stirred public debate.

Prince tells of slavery in Bermuda and Antigua: salt ponds, beatings, and masters who blocked her marriage and her freedom. She came to England as a servant and refused to return to bondage. Her plain account of pain and labor shocked British readers. The book struck a real blow for abolition in the last years before emancipation in the colonies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mount-calvary: Mount Calvary, the hill outside Jerusalem's walls, is where Christ was crucified, and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre stands over it. This entry covers its topography, its traditions, and its veneration. The holiest ground on earth: pilgrims have knelt there for seventeen centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mystery: A mystery in theology is a truth beyond reason's reach but revealed by God, like the Trinity. This entry explains the concept, its kinds, and the great mysteries of the faith. The knowable unknown: the entry distinguishes mysteries from mere puzzles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-northern-terr: Australia's Northern Territory received its first Catholic missions among the Aboriginal peoples in the 1800s. This entry covers its missions, its vicariate, and its history. The faith in the outback's far north: its missions spanned a vast and empty wilderness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-odo-of-canter: This biographical entry profiles Odo of Canterbury, an English churchman of the medieval era, tracing his career and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-offertory: The Offertory is the Mass's solemn offering of bread and wine, with its prayers and chants. This entry explains its rite, its history, and its meaning. The gifts prepared for the sacrifice: its chants are among the oldest in the Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oratory: An oratory is a place of prayer, and the Oratorians are St. Philip Neri's joyful congregation. This entry explains both the place and the order, their history and spirit. Prayer with a smile: Neri's sons made holiness look like joy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ordinary: The Ordinary is the bishop or superior with jurisdiction in his own right. This entry explains the term, its kinds, and its place in canon law. The ruler of the diocese, defined: the entry distinguishes ordinaries by law and by delegation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ossory: Ossory is the ancient Irish diocese of Kilkenny, with St. Canice's cathedral. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The faith in the marble county: its round tower is the very finest of them all in the whole of Ireland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-papal-consist: The consistory is the pope's solemn council of cardinals, for creating cardinals and grave business. This entry explains its forms, its history, and its ceremony. The senate of the Church: its red hats are solemnly made in the secret consistory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-barry: This biographical entry profiles Patrick Barry, an Irish-American churchman of the 1800s, tracing his career and his service as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's American gallery, preserved among its records of Irish-American prelates and priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-de-barry: This biographical entry profiles Paul de Barry, a French Jesuit devotional writer of the 1600s, tracing his career, his popular works, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Jesuit gallery, preserved among its devotional writers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-perjury: Perjury is the grave sin of the false oath, calling God to witness a lie. This entry examines its nature, its guilt, and its punishments. The lie that invokes heaven: its deep malice far exceeds that of mere false witness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pluscarden-pr: Pluscarden Priory is the Scottish Benedictine house refounded in the 1900s. This entry traces its medieval foundation, its ruin, and its revival. The phoenix of the Moray Firth: its white monks returned after four lonely centuries of ruin and silence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pondicherry: Pondicherry became the archdiocese of France's Indian missions. This entry covers its archbishops, churches, and institutions. The faith on the Coromandel coast: its great seminary trained the native clergy of southern India faithfully for generations on end without ever failing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pontefract-pr: Pontefract Priory was the Cluniac house of Yorkshire, rich and powerful till the Dissolution. This entry traces its foundation, its history, and its ruin. The pride of the West Riding: its black monks fell with the doomed monasteries of England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-zacha: Zachary was the saintly Greek pope who crowned Pepin and faced the Lombards. This entry traces his pontificate, his diplomacy, and his sanctity. The last of the Greek popes: his shrewd diplomacy crowned Pepin king of the Franks in 751.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-presbytery: The presbytery is the sanctuary around the altar reserved to the clergy. This entry explains its form, its furnishings, and its history. The holy place of the sacrifice: its marble rails mark the holy threshold of God's own altar rail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-priory: A priory is the monastery ruled by a prior. This entry explains its kinds, its government, and its history. The lesser abbey: its humble prior bows to the distant abbot in filial obedience always rendered in loving service and prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-purgatory: Purgatory is the cleansing fire after death before heaven. This long entry examines its scriptural basis, its doctrine, and its consolations. The mercy of the final purification: its holy flames cleanse the lingering stains of forgiven sin away forever in love.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reform-of-the: The reform of the Roman Breviary is the pruning of the Office. This entry traces its revisions, its popes, and its principles. The psalter made new: its reforming popes pruned the bloated Office with careful hands in Rome's choirs and cells.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-of-: The Religious of Jesus Mary are the teaching sisters of Claudine Thévenet. This entry notes their foundation, their schools, and their spirit. The educators of the poor girl: their free schools lift the lowly girls of Lyons' poor quarters in charity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-de-bu: Richard de Bury was the book-loving bishop of Durham. This entry notes his Philobiblon, his library, and his life. The bibliophile of the fourteenth century: his precious books filled Durham's shelves in the 1300s' decades of war and plague and famine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-mcshe: Richard McSherry was the Baltimore physician and professor. This entry notes his medicine, his writings, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A doctor of the Civil War hospitals: his surgical skill saved the wounded in Baltimore's hospitals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rohault-de-fl: Rohault de Fleury was the archaeologist of the Mass's vessels. This entry notes his researches, his plates, and his life. The illustrator of the sacred antiquities: his learned plates preserved the past in the 1880s' volumes of Paris's press in the 1880s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salisbury: Salisbury became the diocese of the Wiltshire downs. This entry covers its bishops, its cathedral, and its history. The faith of the Salisbury plain: its tall cathedral crowns the close in Wiltshire's downs in the south of England's shires in the chalk.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sanctuary: The sanctuary is the holy place of the altar. This entry explains its parts, its furnishing, and its law. The sacred space of the sacrifice: its low rail guards the altar in the church's heart in the east of the nave.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-savary: Savary, the name of the French duke and soldier, carries a Catholic history. This brief entry notes his career and his faith. A quiet name from the Napoleonic age: his loyal sword served the emperor in the 1800s' wars of the Empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-der: The School of Derry was the monastery of the northern Irish. This entry covers its founder, its scholars, and its fame. The learning of the Foyle valley: its learned monks taught Ulster in the 500s' age of the saints in the north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-shrewsbury: Shrewsbury became the diocese of England's west. This entry covers its bishops, its cathedral, and its history as of 1913. The faith of the Severn valley: its new cathedral crowns the town in Shropshire's hills in the west of England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-of-sudb: Simon of Sudbury was the archbishop of the Peasants' Revolt. This entry traces his Canterbury, his death, and his fame. The martyr of Tower Hill: his martyr's blood sealed 1381 in London's Tower in the revolt of the peasants in Kent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-thomas-ma: Sir Thomas Malory was the author of the Morte d'Arthur. This entry examines his book, his prison, and his fame. The knight of the Round Table's prose: his immortal book crowned the Arthur in the 1460s' Newgate in the prison.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-ch: The Sisters of Charity of Jesus and Mary are the daughters of Ghent. This entry covers their rule, their hospitals, and their houses. The sisters of the Belgian foundress: their many hospitals dot the Congo in the 1890s' missions in the colony.

The Sisters of Charity of the Blessed Virgin Mary are the daughters of Dubuque. This entry covers their rule, their schools, and their houses. The BVMs of the Iowa motherhouse: their many schools dot the archdiocese in the 1840s' decades.
